issues.issue: Section 1 says the Employment Period ends "as provided in Section 4", but Section 4(a) fixes no term or expiry date while Section 4(b) speaks of termination "during the term of this Agreement". The gap leaves the duration of the instrument open to construction.

"Reasonable best efforts", "full business time" and the carve-out for "a reasonable amount of time to charitable or other similar activities" set no measurable boundary, and the catch-all "or other similar activities" has uncertain reach against the enumerated "charitable".

Section 9 (Other Businesses) forbids Employee from being "engaged in, render[ing] services for, or permit[ting] his or her name to be used in connection with any business other than the business of the Company", which is hard to square with 2(b)'s express permission to devote time to charitable or similar activities.

The clause sets a commencement date but no ending date or renewal mechanism, so "Term" has no content beyond the listed termination events. Whether the Agreement is at-will indefinitely is left to construction.
Section 4(b) conditions severance on termination "during the term of this Agreement", but Section 4(a) never fixes any such term, so the two cannot be read together without supplying a term.

It is unclear whether "entitled to receive his or her Base Salary ... during the twelve (12) month period" means twelve months of salary continuation or something less, and the mitigation cut-off keyed to being "employed ... on a full-time basis" and to being "in breach of Sections 5, 6 or 7" (breach determined by whom, and on what standard) invites argument.
Severance is payable only on termination "during the term of this Agreement", yet Section 4(a) fixes no term, leaving the condition precedent unanchored in the instrument.

Section 4(c) limits an employee terminated for Cause or on resignation/death/Disability to "only ... Base Salary through the date of termination", while Section 20 promises the unpaid Sign-On Bonus in full on exactly those events. The two cannot both be applied literally.

Section 4(d) cuts off all rights to "bonuses ... and other compensation" after termination except as provided in Section 4(b), but Section 20 expressly makes the unpaid Sign-On Bonus payable within 30 days after termination and Section 19 accelerates equity on a post-Change-of-Control termination.

"Any physical or mental incapacitation which results in Employee's inability to perform his or her duties ... for a total of 120 days" does not say whether partial incapacity counts, and the CEO's "good faith judgment" is the only measure. The deeming date in (ii) also assumes a continuous rather than aggregate 120 days.

Clause (i) runs "conviction of a felony or any other act or omission involving dishonesty, disloyalty or fraud", so the general words sit against a criminal-conviction specific and their reach is uncertain, and (v) "any other material breach of this Agreement" is an open catch-all after four enumerated grounds. "Conduct tending to bring the Company ... into substantial public disgrace or disrepute" is also vague on its face.

"Confidential Information" is defined as all "information, observations and data ... concerning the business or affairs" obtained while employed, with no time limit and no exclusion for the employee's general skill and knowledge, so its boundary against the public-domain proviso is contestable.

"Work Product" covers anything relating to the Company's "actual or anticipated business ... or existing or future products or services", a boundary that cannot be fixed at the time of creation. The clause declares ownership rather than assigning, leaving the mechanism of transfer to construction.

Clause (iv) bars Participation in "any business in which he would be reasonably likely to employ, reveal, or otherwise utilize Trade Secrets" in "any geographical area in which the Company or any of its affiliates conduct business" — "reasonably likely" and the trade-secret trigger have no ascertainable boundary, and "the Executive" is a term the Agreement never defines. "Participate" is then given an open-ended "or otherwise" catch-all after a long enumerated list.

Section 7(b) asserts the covenant has a fixed "geographical area" and that the Company operates worldwide, while 7(a)(iv) limits the restraint to areas where the Company conducts business; the two descriptions of scope pull apart.

The recital-style acknowledgment that the covenant is reasonable in "duration, geographical area and scope" and worldwide sits against Section 7(a)(iv), whose geographic reach is defined only by where the Company happens to do business, and against Section 7(c), which contemplates a court finding those very restrictions unreasonable.

Section 12 (Severability) directs that an unenforceable provision be treated "as if such invalid, illegal or unenforceable provision had never been contained herein", while 7(c) directs the court instead to substitute the maximum reasonable restriction. The two remedies for an overbroad covenant point in opposite directions.

"[M]oney damages may not be an adequate remedy" is a permissive, hedged formulation that does not concede irreparable harm, and "until such breach or violation has been duly cured" gives the tolling no fixed endpoint. Both are terms an injunction application would turn on.

The recited consideration for the restrictive covenants is "(ii) additional good and valuable consideration as set forth in this Agreement", which identifies nothing specific and leaves the sufficiency of consideration for Sections 5-7 open to argument.

The bar on becoming "engaged in, render[ing] services for, or permit[ting] his or her name to be used in connection with any business other than the business of the Company" is unqualified, so whether it reaches unpaid, charitable or passive involvement is uncertain.

Section 2(b) expressly permits Employee to devote "a reasonable amount of time to charitable or other similar activities", which Section 9's absolute prohibition without written consent appears to withdraw.

Severability treats an unenforceable provision as "never ... contained herein", whereas Section 7(c) requires a court to substitute the maximum reasonable period, scope or area, and Section 7(b) says the covenants survive an order terminating other provisions. The competing reformation regimes must be reconciled.

The integration clause supersedes "any prior understandings, agreements or representations ... which may have related to the subject matter hereof", yet Section 19 presupposes the continuing force of the Equity Agreements with Parent and 19(f) preserves them. Whether the equity documents are superseded or preserved is left unclear.

"Each of the Company's affiliates are intended third party beneficiaries" would let Parent and other affiliates enforce, which sits awkwardly with Section 19, where the Incentive Equity obligations run against Parent under the Equity Agreements rather than against the Company. Who may sue on which promise is not clearly allocated.

The parties submit to the "co-exclusive jurisdiction" of the federal and state courts named — a term of no settled meaning that could be read as exclusive, or as merely consensual and non-exclusive. The word choice is the sort of drafting slip that decides a forum motion.

Subsection (a) is purely definitional and grants no vesting, yet Section 19(c) refers to "the vesting provided in subsection (a) above" and Section 19(d) to "the accelerated vesting provided for in each of Sections 19(a) and 19(b)". The internal cross-references cannot be made to fit 19(a) as written.

Section 19(d) applies pro rata treatment to "the accelerated vesting provided for in each of Sections 19(a) and 19(b)", but the acceleration provisions are in fact 19(b) and 19(c), so whether this subsection is the one captured is uncertain.

The parenthetical directs the calculation to be made "after giving effect to the vesting provided in subsection (a) above", but subsection (a) provides no vesting at all — the intended reference is plainly to 19(b). The mis-citation changes how the additional fifty percent is computed.

The pro rata rule is tied to "the accelerated vesting provided for in each of Sections 19(a) and 19(b)", yet 19(a) accelerates nothing and the second acceleration sits in 19(c), so the cross-reference is off by one subsection. Whether the pro rata strip applies to the 19(c) acceleration is therefore open.

The definition labels two different limbs "(ii)" and the third limb is a garbled duplication of the same text, so the numbering and the boundary of the third trigger cannot be read off the page. The scope of an event as consequential as a Change of Control turns on this defective enumeration.

The clause preserves "the Option Agreements", a term the Agreement never defines; the defined term introduced in Section 19(a) is "Equity Agreements". Whether the saving clause covers all Equity Agreements or only option documents is left to construction.

The trigger reads "payable in full within 30 days upon the Employee's resignation, death or Disability ... and if the Employee is terminated by the Company at any time with or without Cause" — the conjunction "and" makes it unclear whether the two limbs are alternatives or cumulative conditions. The word choice decides whether a for-Cause termination pays the balance.

Section 4(c) limits a for-Cause or resignation/death/Disability termination to "only ... Base Salary through the date of termination" and Section 4(d) cuts off all rights to bonuses accruing after termination except under 4(b), while this section makes the unpaid Bonus payable in full on precisely those events.
